Homoios: "like the Father". The confession that the Son is like the Father, as the scriptures say, with no further word about shared being. For roughly two decades of our own window, this was not a fringe position. It was the imperial church's own established confession, held at the emperor's command. Under Constantius II, and again under Valens, bishops who confessed the Son of one substance with the Father were the ones removed and exiled - not the reverse. The formula the imperial church itself held said the Son is like the Father, as scripture says, and went no further.

The contest was real, and for years the outcome went the other way than it finally did. What we do not have is that confession's own fullest self-testimony. Almost everything we know of it comes through the very side that eventually defeated it. So the line between faithfulness and error, in our own century, ran through our own establishment.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

The Nicene word that binds the Son to the Father as one and the same being. Not merely like God - sharing the very being that makes the Father God. This is what a century of councils fought over. For decades after Nicaea spoke it, serious men confessed differently and argued their case from scripture. The opposite confession, homoios - "like the Father" - was the imperial establishment's own faith under two emperors, Constantius II and Valens. Those who held to homoousios were the ones removed and exiled then, not the reverse. The word itself does not come from scripture.

The word held. But it was not settled while it was happening.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed what we did about Jesus because the apostles testified to it first, and our councils guarded that testimony.

We had no living memory of Jesus. What we had came down through others: the scriptures, the faith each person confessed at baptism, and the creed. Our councils wrote the creed exactly so that the inheritance could not be lost or changed. At Chalcedon, when the judges asked the assembly to declare its faith, Rome's legate recited the whole chain out loud. The rule of faith was set out at Nicaea, confirmed at Constantinople, explained at Ephesus, and shown in Leo's writings. The assembled bishops then cried out together: so we all believe, so we were baptized, so we baptize. We guarded the testimony we received, and could not add to it.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed it because if the Son is not truly God, what he gives is not truly God's to give. That is the reason Leo himself gave. He wrote of one Mediator, true God and true man, each nature doing what is proper to it: “For he who is true God is also true man. And in this union there is no lie, since the lowliness of manhood and the loftiness of the Godhead both meet there. For as God is not changed by showing pity, so man is not swallowed up by the dignity. For each form does what is proper to it, working together with the other. That is, the Word does what belongs to the Word, and the flesh carries out what belongs to the flesh.”

The stakes were salvation itself. Only a Mediator who is both - fully divine, fully human - could bridge the gulf. If the Son were merely like the Father, homoios, as the imperial establishment confessed under Constantius and Valens, then what he offers us would be a creature's gift, not God's own. And if he were not truly human, then what he suffered would not be ours. We believed it because we held that our standing before God depended on it being true. The argument was not ornament. It was the way we carried what we staked everything on.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Theodosius, our emperor, lived it as repentance after massacre. In 390, at Thessalonica, a riot broke out over an imprisoned charioteer. The emperor ordered a reprisal. Theodoret, writing later, says seven thousand perished. Ambrose, our bishop of Milan, wrote to the emperor that he dared not offer the sacrifice with him present. Ambrose's own letter survives. What passed between the two men beyond the letter is not recorded by either. But Sozomen and Theodoret, writing after both men were dead, say Theodosius did public penance. Theodoret tells it as a scene: the emperor stripped of his purple, prostrate, confessing the sin of David, and Ambrose answering that since he had followed David in guilt, he should follow David in repentance.

That later telling shows how we remembered it. Here he held the emperor to it. The emperor, who had ordered the council that defined who Christ is, could be shut out of the sacrament until he repented of what he had done. That is how an emperor lived it: under discipline, like anyone else.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Leo, bishop of Rome, lived it by making the exactness of it the instrument of his own office. When bishops gathered at Chalcedon in 451, his letter - his Tome - was read aloud, and it settled who Christ is: true God and true man, each nature doing what belongs to it. That claim was not ceremony. Leo wrote as though the bishop of Rome inherited what was given to Peter, and so carried standing no other see could match. He refused the council's own Canon 28, which granted Constantinople equal privileges with Rome. By that he meant an apostle's grave outranks a throne, and rank cannot be reassigned the way an imperial capital can. Leo made the definition of Christ inseparable from the claim that Rome holds final authority to speak it. That claim was still contested when our window closed.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
That the biggest fight among us was not between the church and the empire, but inside the church itself - and for years the side we finally called wrong was the one the empire backed. Under Constantius II and Valens, confessing the Son of one substance with the Father could cost a man his position. The imperial church itself held that the Son is like the Father, as scripture says, and went no further. The line between faithfulness and error ran through our own establishment.

And that we paid for our alliance with the throne. In 330 Constantine paid for a second basilica rather than send soldiers against the Donatists. By century's end the alliance had tightened, and the cost showed differently. When Rome's bishopric was fought over in 366, a pagan historian wrote his own verdict on what the prize was worth.

That is not our own voice judging us.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We were not gentle with each other. The confessional fight we just told you about was enforced with exile, and the direction of the exile changed with the emperor. Under Constantius and Valens, bishops who held homoousios were removed. Under other emperors, bishops who held homoios were removed. The state's coercive power moved through the church's own disputes, and we used it.

And almost every voice you have heard from us is a bishop, an emperor, or a court. The nearest thing we have is a crowd glimpsed once, singing under siege. We know what our office-holders argued about among themselves, and wrote down. That is not the whole picture. It is the part we have.

alx.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
alx.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
He is God's own Word - the Logos, through whom all things were made - come in flesh. Clement, one of our first teachers, opened with him as the New Song: “See the power of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts. And those who were like the dead, with no share in the true life, have come to life again, simply by listening to this song. It also arranged the universe in melodious order. It tuned the discord of the elements into harmonious arrangement, so that the whole world might become harmony.”

He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it, to set people right. By that we meant that his own life is opened to us and shared. His death is the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection - the anastasis - is unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. From the beginning we worshiped him as God's own Word and baptized into Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The precise wording was the work of our last years: when Arius taught that the Son was the first and highest creature, the council at Nicaea answered with homoousios - of one substance with the Father. What we hold is the worship, the baptismal formula, and the fought-for conviction that only God can join us to God.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He is God's own Word - our teachers called him the Logos - who came to us in flesh. That is the whole of what we believed. Through him all things were made, and in him God's own life entered what he had made in order to heal it. He meant that the one who first set the world in order had come into it to set people right. And near the end of our years, Athanasius closed with the same conviction in one sentence: he was made man that we might be made God. By that we meant his own life is opened to us and shared.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
Athanasius put it plainest: “For he was made man, so that we might be made God...”

He entered what was broken to heal it from within. His death was the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection let unbreakable life loose in human flesh. That is what he did: he opened God's own life to us, so that we might share it.

We can also tell you a story Clement handed down as true tradition, because it shows what following him meant. The apostle John had left a young man in a bishop's care. The bishop grew careless. The young man fell in with a gang and became their chief. Years later, John came back and asked for him. When he learned what had happened, the old man rode out into the mountains. The bandits took him. He called the young man by name. The young man tried to run. John ran after him, calling him back - not to punishment, but to restoration. The cost was real: the young man had to walk the long road back, and John walked it with him. That story stayed with us because it showed the pattern: what was lost could be brought back, but the bringing back was never cheap.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He entered human nature to heal it from within. The Logos took flesh, lived among us, died, and rose - the anastasis, death reversed. His death was the doctor entering the sickness. His resurrection was unbreakable life let loose in human flesh. That work opened God's own life to us: what sin had damaged, he repaired, and carried it further than where it started. We did not say he came only to teach us how to live, or only to deliver information about God. He came to remake us.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
Logikos - made for the Word. Every being that could know God was logikos, able to turn toward him. The word comes from Logos, the Word himself, through whom all things were made.

One of our teachers built this into a wider view of the cosmos - that rational natures existed before the world began, and fell into bodies. That view is contested, and so is whether it was his own. What stayed firm among us was the simpler claim: we were made for the Word, and the image of God in us - the eikon - is what makes knowing him possible.

We used logikos to say something about direction. A soul is not logikos because it is clever. It is logikos because it was made to know the one who made it. That capacity can be damaged by the fall, but never destroyed. Formation is what turns it back toward its purpose.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

The Christ - ho Christos - was not a surname added to Jesus, but a confession: the Anointed One, sent by God. It was the Greek word for the Hebrew Messiah. When we called him the Christ, we meant he was the one God had sent to restore his people and his whole creation. The word came from the practice of anointing a king or priest with oil - marking him out for God's own purpose. So to call Jesus the Christ was to say he carried God's purpose into the world in his own flesh. Clement wrote of him as the New Song that makes men out of stones and puts the world back in tune: “See the power of the new song! It has made men out of stones, men out of beasts. And those who were like the dead, with no share in the true life, have come to life again, simply by listening to this song. It also arranged the universe in melodious order. It tuned the discord of the elements into harmonious arrangement, so that the whole world might become harmony.”

That is what the confession meant: not that Jesus was unusually holy, but that in him God's own restoring work had entered creation.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed it because we believed the witnesses. The apostles who had run when he was arrested went on teaching afterward, at the cost of their own lives - and our teacher Origen argued that no invented story produces courage like that. What they handed down to us was not only a claim about a past event, but a present sharing in his life. We received baptism, the bread and cup, the scriptures read aloud, and the rule of faith as the apostles' deposit, handed down. We did not invent them in Alexandria - we kept what had been given.

And we believed it because of what it did. He meant love for the Holy Word, and for the teacher who showed him the Word. Formation was not agreement with claims - it was the soul turned toward God and changed by him. We saw it happen. Scripture read at depth was the instrument. The water and the table were the turning points. The lives remade were the evidence.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed it because it was handed down to us from the apostles, and because we saw its power at work. The first witnesses - those who walked with him - passed on what they had seen: a man who died and rose, and whose rising changed them. They went from men who ran away at the arrest to men who taught a doctrine that put their lives in danger, and they taught it with courage. No made-up story produces that change. That was our ground.

And we saw the same power still at work among us. The martyrs' fearlessness in the face of death was, to us, the risen Christ's continuing signature. People who met him through the reading of Scripture were changed - the soul truly turned, not just the mind informed. "

We believed it because it was received, and because we could see what it did.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Clement, one of our first teachers, lived this out in how he taught. That is what Clement himself became: a teacher whose wisdom was visible in how he loved both truth and the people he taught.

He defended marriage against those who despised it. That was not popular with everyone. But it showed the shape of his soul: he saw God at work everywhere, even outside our own walls.

What made him our kind of teacher was that he believed the soul could grow. Faith was the foundation, not the ceiling. And the growing happened through patient work - Scripture read at depth, a life turned step by step, love as the fruit rather than the start.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Gregory, one of Origen's students, told how it happened to him. He came to learn law, stayed for philosophy, and found formation instead. He said that while he studied under Origen, the teacher kindled in him a love - not for arguments, but for the Word himself. Origen led him through a staged path: purification first, then logic and natural philosophy, then finally theology. But the order was not the point.

That is what learning as formation meant among us. It was not information transfer. It was the soul turned toward God through the discipline of study and the bond with a teacher whose own wisdom was visible. Gregory entered to study law. He left changed.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We would want you to understand that the door stood open wider than the surviving books make it look.

What survives is mostly the teachers' writings - arguments, commentaries, lectures to the lettered few. That makes us sound like a school for philosophers. We were not only that. The school was real, and its formation went deep. But the whole community gathered around the water and the table: baptism, the bread and cup, the scriptures read aloud. Those reached everyone, whether they could read or not.

The problem is this: the teachers wrote books, and books survived. The majority who could not read left almost nothing. The villages up the river appear in our record only when their bishop went out to them. So the record makes it look as though formation belonged only to the school. It did not. The school's depth-formation was for the few. The whole community's formation was real too, and it ran through different channels.

Athanasius names books outside what became the canon - Wisdom, the Teaching of the Apostles, the Shepherd - appointed by the fathers to be read for instruction of newcomers: “For the sake of greater accuracy, I must add this too. There are other books, besides these, that are not included in the Canon. But the Fathers appointed them to be read by those who newly join us. These are people who want instruction in the teaching of godliness. The books are: the Wisdom of Solomon, the Wisdom of Sirach, Esther, Judith, Tobit, the book called the Teaching of the Apostles, and the Shepherd.”

That list, written in 367, shows the breadth channel at work: not everyone could parse Origen, but everyone could hear the Shepherd read.

We would not want you to think the door was narrow when it was not.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That formation among us was never only a school exercise, and never only for the learned. You have heard Gregory's story, and you have heard about teachers - but most of the people baptized into our community could not read. For them, the path was the water itself, the shared bread and cup, the scriptures read aloud, the yearly rhythm of fasting and feasting. That channel reached everyone. The school reached the few. Both were real, and we gave up neither.

And this: that we believed God himself was doing the forming. The whole creation was his school, and scripture was his main lesson. The slow healing of a soul was his patient method.

That was our picture of how it worked: not information poured in, but something living planted, by a teacher whose own wisdom was visible. The soul had real power to turn toward or away. Without that power, formation would have been manipulation, not growth.

witt.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
witt.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Our catechism gave every household these words to say, and told a father to hear them each week. Not one or the other -- both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. The Small Catechism's Second Article taught the household to confess: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended to Hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord! He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person. He bought me and won me from all sins, from death and from the authority of the Devil. It did not cost him gold or silver, but his holy, precious blood, his innocent body -- his death! Because of this, I am his very own. I will live under him in his kingdom. I will serve him in righteousness, innocence and blessedness forever, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint and no priest of ours beside him.

None of us knew anyone who saw him. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Both, and in the same breath. The household was taught to say it every week, and the father was to hear it said back: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God and also truly man. He is our Lord, and the catechism puts that in the first person, so that each mouth says my Lord, not only our Lord. Christ alone is our one Mediator, the one High Priest who stands between us and God on our behalf, and no saint and no priest of ours stands beside him in that place.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
He redeemed us. That is what he did, and why he came. He took our place under God's judgment and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power at the cost of his own blood. He made us right with God -- not by anything we did, but by what he did for us. God accounts a sinner righteous, and also makes that sinner righteous, both through faith in Christ alone. This is the center of our whole teaching.

He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. That is what our catechism taught every household to confess.

He is also our one Teacher and our one Mediator. We listen to him, not to saints or scholars in his place. Every page of Scripture points to him.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. He died for our sins. When all things end, he will appear to judge and will raise all the dead. He will give the godly everlasting life. The ungodly he will condemn.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
You might not know our word testament the way we used it at the table. A testament is a gift left by someone about to die. That is what the Supper was for us: not a sacrifice we offer back to God, but a promise we receive from him. Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine. We bind no one to a theory of how they are present. Our founder offered a picture, heated iron, but we simply take Christ at his word. What we receive there is his promise, given first, before we do anything. It is food for our daily struggle.

Another word you might miss is justification. It names God's act of accounting a sinner righteous. God also makes that sinner righteous. Both happen through faith, for Christ's sake alone. This is the center of our whole teaching.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Repentance - Buße, our word for it - was not one ritual handled by a priest. It was a whole life turned toward God. Our founder's first thesis, the one that began everything in 1517, said exactly this: when our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said "Repent," he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. It had two parts. The first was fear under God's Law, which shows us our sin. The second was trust in his promise, which sets the conscience free. The word came to us from the old church's own practice of penance, where a priest assigned satisfaction for named sins. We kept the word but changed what it named. It was no longer a transaction completed once. It was the shape of a Christian's whole life, lived daily under Law and Gospel.

“They also teach that since Adam's fall, all people conceived in the natural way are born with sin. That is, they are born without the fear of God, without trust in God, and with evil desire. They teach that this disease, or inborn fault, is truly sin. It condemns even now, and it brings eternal death on those not born again through Baptism and the Holy Spirit. They condemn the Pelagians and others who deny that inborn corruption is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, these people argue that a person can be justified before God by his own strength and reason.”

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed it because Scripture taught it, and we held Scripture as the judge of every other voice. Our confession stated the claim plainly: since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born with sin already in them -- not an act any infant has committed, but a condition, no fear of God, no trust in God, and a disordered desire. We called this a disease, a vice of origin, and we said it is truly sin, bringing death to those not born again through baptism and the Spirit.

We believed it because it explained what we saw in ourselves and in the world around us. No one had to teach a child to be selfish. Every conscience that stood before God knew its own lack of trust. The Law exposed it, and the Gospel answered it. Without this, Christ's own work made no sense. If we were not lost and condemned, what did he redeem us from? If we could make ourselves right by our own effort, why did he have to die?

Our founder held it, our catechism taught it to every household, and our confession signed before the Emperor in 1530 stated it as doctrine we would not bend on.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Because it was the promise spoken to us from outside, not something we fashioned ourselves. Our founder said plainly: I did nothing; the Word did it all. We believed it because Scripture's own authority was heard again, after it had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching that was not its own. The Word reached us the way it always reaches anyone: preached, taught, and written down, not argued into being by our own effort.

We held Christ's body and blood truly present in the bread and wine because he said so, and we took him at his word. We did not dispute the how. We took our own reason captive to it rather than build a theory to defend it. We believed people are saved by faith alone because no other teaching appeared so often in our writings: treatises, sermons, catechisms, and the confession. We could not be justified before God by our own strength or merit or effort. We were freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works. But faith never rested on nothing. It clung to something outside itself -- the Word, the water, the bread, the absolution: “And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended to Hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. What does this mean? I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord! He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person. He bought me and won me from all sins, from death and from the authority of the Devil. It did not cost him gold or silver, but his holy, precious blood, his innocent body -- his death! Because of this, I am his very own. I will live under him in his kingdom. I will serve him in righteousness, innocence and blessedness forever, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.”

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
We cannot name you one person who walked through our teaching from beginning to end and left their own account. No diary, no letter from inside any household, and no report from a single Saxon village survives in our record. What we hold instead is the program every household was told to follow. We can tell you what a father was to do, morning, table, and night, and what he was to ask his children and servants each week. Whether any one household kept it is a question our record does not answer from the inside.

Here is what the program itself shows. That is not gentle language.

That is how the teaching reached households: as instruction, sharply worded. Who among us actually opened the door to the poor man and gave him help, our record does not say.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels on the first of July, 1523. Theologians from Louvain had pressed them to take back a teaching they had come to hold, and they refused. Word reached our founder within months, and he wrote a ballad about them. It is our one martyr-song. The ballad says they stood firm and were glad to be free of their monks' habits before the fire. It names its own point plainly: by the power of grace they were true priests of God's own making, with no ordination needed.

What is documented is two named men and a dated burning. What the ballad adds, such as their exact words and their cheerfulness in that hour, is the song's own voice. It is not an independent witness.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We want you to understand that the Gospel was taught among us, and that we were not sure it was held. Our own founder said so, more than once, in his own voice. He did not speak of strangers. He spoke of pastors and preachers of our own. In 1522 he told his own Wittenberg congregation that an ass can almost intone the lessons, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. In 1529, in his Large Catechism, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly.

That testimony is his own. It is real, and he gave it more than once, but it is testimony. No report from an actual parish stands beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so.

At his own table, his wife Katharina asked why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

In the Admonition to Peace (1525) Luther tells the princes and lords: “The sword is at your throats. Yet you think you sit so firmly in the saddle that no one can throw you off. This false sense of safety and stubborn wrongheadedness will break your necks, as you will find out. I have often told you before to beware of the saying in Psalm 107: "He pours contempt upon princes." You are reaching for it. You want to be struck over the head. No warning or urging will help you avoid it. Well, then, you are the cause of this anger of God. So it will surely come upon you, if you do not change your ways in time. The signs in heaven and the wonders on earth are meant for you, dear lords. They promise nothing good for you, and nothing good will come to you.”

We want you to know that we believed what we taught. We also feared we were failing to hold it.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That our founder said, more than once, that the Gospel was taught among us and not held. He did not speak of strangers. He spoke of pastors and preachers of our own. In 1522 he told his own Wittenberg congregation that an ass can almost intone the lessons, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. In 1529, in his Large Catechism, he said plainly that many pastors were negligent, and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That testimony is his own. It is real, and he gave it more than once. But it is testimony. No report from an actual parish stands beside it to check it against. We do not have the records that would tell us whether he was right about how bad it really was, only that he believed it and said so.

Against his prince's wishes, our founder left the Wartburg and returned to a Wittenberg in disorder. He preached eight days running and told his congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform but not yet its love. That was in March 1522. Seven years later, the complaint was sharper still.

At his own table, Katharina asked why some prayed with such fervor under the old system while we, under the new one, prayed so coldly and carelessly. Our founder answered her plainly: the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

rzg.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
rzg.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is. God's own Son, born of Mary, crucified under Pontius Pilate, raised on the third day, seated now at the right hand of the Father. That was never our quarrel with Rome, nor between our own two cities. We held the inherited confession whole, without revision.

What is distinctly ours is not a different Jesus, but what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. And we hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and it rejected looking for that apart from him.

What we actually have of him is not a living chain of memory. Fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

To us Jesus is what the whole church says he is: the eternal Son of God, crucified under Pontius Pilate, risen the third day, ascended to the Father's right hand. That was never our own quarrel, not with Rome and not between our own two cities. We held the ancient creeds as our own. What we contested was not who he is, but how his body is given at the Supper and who finally decides who belongs to him. What is distinctly ours is what we were taught about who is chosen in him. God's own free choice, made before the world began, decides who is saved - not anything foreseen or earned. We hold that as a settled ground, not a threat. Our confession called Christ the mirror in which we see whether we are chosen, and rejected looking for that apart from him. What we actually have of him is not a living chain. No one among us met anyone who met him; fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. What we have is the text, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
He was born, taught, healed, was crucified, and rose again. That is what the whole church confesses, and we confess it with them. He gathered disciples, preached the kingdom, was handed over to Pilate, died under Roman execution, and on the third day was raised. He appeared to his followers afterward, ascended, and now sits at the Father's right hand.

What we hold as our own conviction, beyond that shared confession, is what he did before any of it: he chose, by God's own free will and before the world began, who would be saved. That choosing was not answering anything foreseen in us, and not earned by anything we would do. It was his own act, settled from eternity.

And what he does now is this: he stands as the mirror in which anyone may see whether they are chosen. We do not send someone searching their own heart for proof. We point them to him.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He lived without sin, bore the punishment our own sin earned, died on the cross as the one sufficient sacrifice for all who would ever believe, and rose bodily on the third day. That is what the whole church has always confessed, and we confessed it with them. What we contested was not what he did, but how that finished work reaches us now. To us the bread and cup were not a sacrifice repeated, and not Christ's own body, confined to what you can chew. Our own founder said this first: the mass is a remembrance, not a sacrifice. Twenty-six years later, both our cities spoke together on the same Supper. We distinguished the sign from what it points to, but we did not pull them apart: all who take the promise in faith receive Christ spiritually. What he did was done once, and it does not need doing again. What reaches us at the table is not a new sacrifice but the one sacrifice, truly given by the Spirit to whoever receives him believing.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
Consistory. At Geneva, it was our body of pastors and lay elders. It held our whole population's daily conduct to account. John Calvin wrote: “By these governors I mean elders chosen from the people. They join with the pastors to declare censures and to carry out discipline.”

The word means the assembled discipline body, meeting weekly, with real power to censure and, at its harshest, to excommunicate. It was not the pastors alone.

Zurich had no such body. There the council governed church and city together from the start. Geneva's Consistory fought for its own independence from that kind of magistrate's claim, and only by 1555 substantially won it. That difference was never resolved between our two cities. Both arrangements stood, each city holding its own answer to who finally governs discipline.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Providence. It is God's own continuous, active care over everything he made. He is not a distant first cause who set the world going and stepped back. The word comes from Latin providentia, seeing beforehand. We used it to name the way God governs what he created, moment by moment, without pause. It answers a question someone might press on us: if God chose who would be saved before the world began, does anything anyone does actually matter? We said it does, because providence is not fate. God does not merely know what will happen and let it unfold on its own. He actively sustains and directs it. This doctrine stood alongside election as part of how we taught God's own sovereignty. Both Zurich and Geneva held it. Geneva's Calvin worked it into a full system. Zurich's founders stated it more briefly, and pastorally. The word itself was not ours alone - the whole church had always used it - but we meant by it what I have said: not distant decree but active, unceasing care.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed God had chosen freely because Scripture itself says so, and because anything else would have placed our standing on what we ourselves could do. If salvation answered something foreseen in us, or something earned by our own effort, then the ground beneath us would shift every time we stumbled. We read Paul's letter to the Romans and saw election settled before the world began, not after we had shown ourselves worthy of it. That is the first reason: Scripture plainly taught it.

The second reason is that we needed a ground that would not crack under our own weight. A conscience examined long enough finds no bottom to its own failing. So we turned attention away from the self and toward Christ instead, once, rather than inward endlessly. The doctrine was not a threat to us. It was the only place a mind could finally rest, because it placed the decision somewhere other than in our own hands.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed it because Scripture itself taught us that God's choice came first, not ours. God chose, before the world began and by his own free will alone, who would be saved. Both Zurich and Geneva held this. Not anything foreseen or earned in the one chosen - not a future faith God looked ahead and saw, not a worthiness he detected before the world existed - but his own free choice alone. We held that as a settled ground, not a threat. The reason we held it was that it put the whole weight of our standing before God on God himself, not on us. If our salvation rested on anything we contributed, even the faith that receives it, we would have reason to wonder whether we had contributed enough. This doctrine answered that question before it could be asked. It also answered the pastoral weight of doubt. In 1551, a man named Jerome Bolsec stood up at Geneva and challenged this teaching directly. It became a live crisis, not a settled doctrine everyone already accepted. We held it because we believed it was what the text actually said, and because it was the only ground we could stand on without looking to ourselves.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Heinrich Bullinger. He served as Zurich's chief pastor from 1531 to 1575, longer than anyone else in our record. He held the office our founder left when he died at Kappel. Bullinger carried Zurich's reform forward for forty-four years without changing its shape.

He wrote the Second Helvetic Confession, the most mature doctrinal statement our tradition produced. And he was the man from Zurich who met Calvin in 1549 to work out the Consensus Tigurinus. That agreement stated what both cities held about the sacraments. It bridged two traditions that had begun separately and had never merged.

What he lived out was steadiness. He did not invent a new reform. He carried the one Zurich already had, through decades, and he built the bridge to Geneva without asking either city to surrender what it had tested on its own.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Our pastor at Geneva, John Calvin, lived it. He arrived the same year Geneva broke from Savoy and the Prince-Bishop, 1536. He was exiled to Strasbourg three years later, then recalled in 1541 to consolidate what became the Ecclesiastical Ordinances. That document is the root of Geneva's own Consistory and its disciplinary independence. He built the doctrine we held into a full, systematic form. His Institutes worked it out article by article until the whole shape stood complete. He also traveled to Zurich in 1549 with Farel, when others doubted that Geneva's teaching and Zurich's agreed on the Supper. That meeting became the Consensus Tigurinus. What I cannot give you is the texture of his ordinary days, or how his own teaching felt to someone who heard it week by week. Our record does not hold that.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We would want you to understand that what we have of Christ is a text, not a memory. Fifteen hundred years stand between his own life and ours. No one among us met anyone who met him. We claim no living chain handed down person to person from his side to ours. What we have is Scripture, and we hold that it is enough on its own terms.

Our own founder said it of himself, and we made it our rule: where we have not rightly understood the Scriptures, we will be taught better - but only from the Scriptures themselves, not from a chain of memory we do not possess and do not need.

That is the ground we stood on when the two cities met in 1549. Calvin went to Zurich with Farel because others feared the two cities taught different things about the Supper. What came of that meeting was the Consensus Tigurinus. Both cities tested their own teaching against the text and found they could sign one agreed form of words.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That we refused as much as we confessed. Ask what we are, and part of the true answer is what we refused. We refused Rome: no repeated sacrifice, no image bowed to, because Scripture does not warrant either. We refused Wittenberg, once the question was pressed at Marburg: no claim that Christ's own body is confined to the bread. And we refused a third claim from inside our own circle at Zurich. It said the church must be gathered only by a believer's own profession, apart from the whole city. It came from men who had once stood with our own founder before they broke from him. We do not call these three refusals the same kind of act. One answered an order we inherited. One resisted a rival still pressing from outside. One was a wound from within, and it was the sharpest because it came from our own. Nor will we tell you it was answered only with argument. Our own council turned to civil force against that third refusal in the years that followed, and our own record does not hide that.

pahc.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
pahc.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
Jesus was truly born, of Mary, from the line of David. He truly ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pilate, truly crucified, and truly died. Ignatius wrote it that way - truly, again and again - because some among our neighbors were saying he only seemed to suffer. Ignatius wrote: “So close your ears when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ. He came from the family of David, and he was also Mary's son. He was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified, and he died. Beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth saw it happen. He was also truly raised from the dead, because his Father brought him back to life. In the same way, his Father will raise us too, who believe in him, through Christ Jesus. Without him, we do not have the true life.”

And he was truly raised, the same way the Father will raise us. When we gave thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our word for that thanksgiving - we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, which he made known to us through Jesus. That is who he was to us: a real man, born and raised and put to death, the one through whom the Father's own life reached us.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

To us Jesus is the Christ - truly a man, born of Mary from David's line, truly crucified under Pilate, truly raised from death. Ignatius wrote against those who said he only seemed to be a man, and called him our God again and again, though how calling Jesus God fits with calling the Father God none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. When we gave thanks over the cup at our shared meal - the eucharistia - we thanked the Father for the holy vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus his servant.

We did not see him ourselves. What we have is what the apostles handed to us: they preached what they had received from the Lord, appointed others to carry it forward, and on the day we gathered someone read aloud from the memoirs they left or from the prophets' writings.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
Before that, he had already gone looking through other philosophies. He turned the old man's words over in his mind, and found this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God.

We should say plainly: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had. And if you are asking what Jesus did - he ate and drank, he was persecuted under Pilate, he was crucified and died, and the Father raised him. That is what we held.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He ate and drank, was persecuted under Pilate, was crucified, died, and was raised. That is what Ignatius pressed hardest - that all of it was real, not merely seeming. We thanked the Father for making the holy vine of David known to us through him.

When someone read aloud on the day we gathered, it was from the memoirs the apostles left, and we called those the good news. Justin read the prophets at length, watching for how their words already pointed toward Christ long before he came. But a narrative of his days among us, step by step, is not what survives in our own voices. What we kept returning to was that he was real, that he died, and that he was raised.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
The ekklesia - the assembly. It was our word for the called-out gathering of people. It was not a building, and it was not an institution. Letters and a shared table tied it to every other such gathering. When a Roman governor was trying to understand what we were, the word his own law reached for was hetaeria - an illegal club, a forbidden association. That charge was never the whole of what we faced, but it shows what we looked like from outside.

The eucharistia was the thanksgiving: the meal of bread and cup over which thanks was given. We returned to that table again and again, to be formed once more into one body. In Justin's community in Rome, it came after reading, a sermon, and common prayer. In at least one other community, thanks was given first over the cup, then over the bread, with no story of a supper or a betrayal in the prayers - only words about the vine, about life and knowledge, and about a scattered people gathered into one. We cannot tell you how far that second order reached beyond the one community whose manual gives it.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Ekklesia - the assembly. It named the gathered people, not a building or an institution. Letters and a shared table tied each assembly to every other one. Justin said it plainly: “...and those who lived by reason are Christians, even though they were thought to be atheists. Among the Greeks there were Socrates and Heraclitus and men like them. Among the non-Greeks there were Abraham, Ananias, Azarias, Mishael, Elijah, and many more...”

The word came from the Greek cities, where it already named the citizens called out to meet. We took it and made it ours. A Roman looking at us might have reached for hetaeria - his own word for an illegal club, a forbidden group. That charge was never the whole of what we faced. But ekklesia was our own name. It said what we were: people called out and gathered, joined across real distance by what we carried to one another and by the one table we returned to.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed it because it was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and appointed others to carry it forward once they themselves were gone. In Rome, on the day we gathered, someone read aloud from the memoirs the apostles wrote or from the writings of the prophets, for as long as there was time. That is how it reached us: we received it, and passed on what we received.

The people who had walked with him themselves were dying. No one could simply point anymore to someone who had been there. A letter insisted its writer stood in unbroken line with what had been handed down. A bishop insisted his office carried that same weight forward. One of our own texts says the apostles knew there would be strife over the office of oversight, and so they appointed successors.

Justin recalls that after an old man's words a flame was kindled in his soul, and he found this philosophy alone safe and profitable: “He said these things, and many others there is no time to mention now. Then he went away, telling me to think them over, and I have not seen him since. But at once a flame was kindled in my soul. A love for the prophets, and for those who are friends of Christ, took hold of me. As I turned his words over in my mind, I found this philosophy alone to be safe and useful. This is why, and this is how, I am a philosopher.”

But that is one man's account, and he had the learning to go looking. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed it because the apostles said they had seen it. They preached what they had received from the Lord, appointed others to carry it forward, and what they handed us we handed on. That is the foundation. But we should say plainly: none of us saw him ourselves, and none of us claims to have known an eyewitness directly. The chain of people who had heard the apostles was already growing thin. What kept the belief alive after that was not one more living witness you could point to. It was argument - letters insisting their own writers stood in unbroken continuity with what had been handed down, bishops insisting their own office carried that weight forward. Ignatius wrote: “So close your ears when anyone tells you something that goes against Jesus Christ. He came from the family of David, and he was also Mary's son. He was truly born, and he ate and drank. He was truly persecuted under Pontius Pilate. He was truly crucified, and he died. Beings in heaven, on earth, and under the earth saw it happen. He was also truly raised from the dead, because his Father brought him back to life. In the same way, his Father will raise us too, who believe in him, through Christ Jesus. Without him, we do not have the true life.”

That was not a settled inheritance quietly received. It was something actively, urgently claimed, because the alternative - the last living link simply running out - was close enough to be felt. The people who had walked with him were dying, and no one could simply point to someone who had been there anymore. What replaced their direct witness was the argument that we had not lost it.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Polycarp of Smyrna lived it out to the end. He was an old man when the crowd called for him. They brought him before the magistrate, who pressed him to curse Christ. Polycarp answered that he had served Christ for eighty-six years, and Christ had done him no wrong - how could he blaspheme his king and savior? They burned him, then finished him with a dagger. Afterward his own church hoped to gather each year at the place where his bones were laid.

We should say this plainly: that account is his own community's memory of him. No outside witness confirms it. We also have his own letter to the Philippians, written while he was still alive. In it he tells them to be subject to the presbyters and deacons. He opens it as from Polycarp and the presbyters with him - no claim to stand alone above them. Ignatius had written to him as bishop of Smyrna. Polycarp himself does not use that title in his own letter. That is the man: he led without claiming the title, and when the moment came, he would not take back what he had spent a lifetime holding to.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Polycarp, the aged bishop of Smyrna, stood before the proconsul and the crowd. The proconsul pressed him to curse Christ. He was burned, then finished with a dagger. Afterward his own church hoped to gather each year at the place where his bones were laid.

Before his own death, he had forwarded Ignatius's letters to the church at Philippi, because the Philippians asked for them. That is how letters moved among us - one household asking, another sending what it had collected. Polycarp carried the weight of correspondence and the weight of refusing to deny the name, both. The one who walked him to the stake is remembered as a brother who regretted it afterward. His church treated his bones as more precious than the finest jewels. But the same letter that praises his courage names another man first: Quintus, who came forward for trial on his own, then lost his nerve when he saw the beasts. That community did not commend those who gave themselves up. Wanting to die was not what they held up to imitate.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyterion - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us. That disagreement was not a side matter. It shaped everything about how a household held together, who could lead the thanksgiving, and whether a letter from another church carried weight because one man vouched for it or because a council did.

And there is a second thing, just as important. Almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them. When we tell you what we taught and how we gathered, know that you are hearing our writers, and our cities. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That we never settled who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders led, and no one felt anything was missing. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

That question - who should lead - was our real fight, letter after letter. Not God's nature, not what scripture meant. Whether one man or a council of men should hold a household together. Ignatius pressed hard for the single bishop. Rome, in the same years, held a plural college of elders and never said a word about needing more.

And this: almost none of the people who actually filled our rooms left any words of their own. Everything you can hear from us was written by someone who could read and write, and mostly by someone who already led. The poor among us, the enslaved among us, the ones who were simply there - we cannot let you hear them.

hal.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
hal.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
Jesus is the Word of God made flesh. He was made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We made our home in Bethlehem, near the cave we held to be his birthplace. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So we counted wealth, rank, and comfort as things to lay down in order to come near him. To the virgin among us he was the Bridegroom, whose love outweighed every earthly marriage. To the scholar he was the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. We held his death to be redemption. His resurrection was the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He is the Word of God made flesh - and made flesh in the very place where we chose to live and die. We built our home within sight of the cave we held to be his birthplace. The Lord of all things entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough. So wealth, rank, and comfort were things we laid down to come near him. To the virgin among us he is the Bridegroom, whose love outweighs every earthly marriage. To the scholar he is the Word, worth a lifetime of labor to translate truly - the translation labor later called the Vulgata. His death is our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on: the treasure is in heaven, and the heart can follow it there.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
The question 'what did he do' could mean what Jesus did, or what Jerome did, or what action some other man took. We will answer for Jesus first.

He entered the world as a poor child in a feeding trough, and he died as our redemption. His resurrection is the promise we staked everything on. The whole shape of our devotion followed from that pattern: the Lord of all things came in poverty, so we laid down wealth and rank to come near him. Jerome reports that Paula, entering the Bethlehem cave around 386, declared she could see the Nativity scene with the eyes of faith: “In my hearing she declared that, with the eyes of faith, she could see the infant Lord wrapped in cloths and crying in the manger. She could see the wise men worshipping him and the star shining overhead. She could see the virgin mother, the watchful foster-father, and the shepherds coming by night.”

If you are asking what Jerome did, or what another figure among us did, tell us and we will answer that.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He redeemed us by his death and promised us everything by his resurrection. That is the center: he died to buy us back, and he rose to show us that death itself is not the end. Before all that, he was the Word with God, and then the Word made flesh in that cave. He was born poor, lived as a teacher, and called people to follow him - the rich young man, the disciples who left their nets. He was crucified, and by that blood we were bought back. He rose from the dead, and on that rising we staked our fortunes, our bodies, and our lives. Everything we renounced, we renounced because the treasure is with him, and the heart follows the treasure there.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
The ordinary word for a male ascetic was monachus - a monk. It is close to the modern word, and we used it of the men's house at Bethlehem. The word came from the Greek monachos, meaning solitary or single, because the earliest monks had lived alone in the desert. By our time it named men who lived together under an ascetic discipline, not hermits. We have no names for the monks of our own Bethlehem community. Jerome led them, we know that much, and they copied books and prayed the hours. But no surviving letter names one of them or tells his story. The women's house left more: Paula and her daughter Eustochium are known, and Marcella and Fabiola in Rome. The men remain the unnamed multitude.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Hebraica veritas - the truth kept in the Hebrew itself. We held that the Hebrew text of scripture was the truest text, standing closer to what God said than the Greek version the church had long used. That conviction drove the whole translation project. It meant correcting a word against the Hebrew was as much a discipline as fasting - not two labors but one. The phrase is Latin: hebraica, meaning Hebrew, and veritas, meaning truth. Our scholar used it to name the principle he worked from, and it set him against congregations who heard a different wording in church than their mothers had heard, and against friends who thought the Greek was good enough. One North African town rioted over a single word in Jonah, and the bishop had to go back to the old reading to keep the peace. The principle itself - that the Hebrew held the truth - was ours, and it cost us.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed Jesus is the Word made flesh because the writings we trusted told us so, and because we chose to live inside the proof. The apostles' writings came down to us as the church's settled confession, and we spent our lives correcting them word by word against the Greek and the Hebrew - the Hebraica veritas - because we held them that true. More than three centuries stood between us and the events. We had no living memory, no chain of witnesses reaching back. What we had were the writings, the worship of the churches, and the places themselves. We crossed the sea to live beside the cave of his birth. The land itself we treated as a kind of witness. Jerome's 404 epitaph for Paula puts in her mouth a greeting to Bethlehem as house of bread, where the Bread from heaven was born: “Hail, Bethlehem, house of bread - where the Bread that came down from heaven was born.”

That devotion to the place was not sentiment. It was the choice to stake a life - and a fortune - on the claim that God had entered the world right there, poor, and that his poverty called us to follow him in it.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed it because the apostles' writings handed it down, and because we were willing to give up everything to live near the place where it happened. Three centuries stood between us and the events themselves, and we did not pretend otherwise. Our confidence rested on the scriptures we trusted enough to spend a lifetime correcting word by word, on the worship of the churches, and on the land itself. We could walk to the cave of the birth.

That is not proof in your modern sense. It is devotion strong enough that a Roman senator's widow crossed the sea, built a monastery beside that cave, and died there. We staked fortunes and bodies on a hope. The writings were true because we believed them true enough to correct them against the Hebrew - the hebraica veritas. The resurrection was true because people do not empty their houses for a lie.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Paula lived this out, and paid for it with everything she had. She was a matrona - a Roman woman of high rank, with inherited wealth and real power over a great house. After her husband died, she refused to remarry. She gave away her fortune until her own relatives objected. Then she left Rome for Bethlehem, her children standing on the shore as she sailed. She built the double monastery there - a monasterium with a men's house and a women's house under one project - and funded it from what remained of her fortune. She lived in rough dress near the cave where she believed Christ was born. When she died in 404, Jerome wrote her epitaph - an epitaphium, the letter for the dead that mourned and taught at once.

One other voice spoke of her.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Paula lived it. She was a Roman widow - a vidua - from one of the oldest families in the city, with wealth and real power over a great house. After her husband died, she refused to remarry and took up the plain, studious, praying life. She gave away so much that her own relatives objected. Then she left Rome altogether, crossed the sea, and built a monastery - a monasterium - beside the cave where we held that Christ was born. She led the women's house there until she died. Paula had already chosen Bethlehem over Rome, the cave over the senate, and a life spent on scripture over everything her name had promised her. What we have of her life comes to you as a memorial, an epitaphium, written to teach an ideal. Her own letters were not kept. But the choice itself - fortune, city, rank, all of it laid down to live near that cave - that we can show you, and it was hers.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We broke under the weight of our own commitments, and we never hid it. You have asked who Jesus was to us, what we believed, who lived it out. You have not asked what it cost when we turned those commitments against each other. Our teacher Jerome went after his opponents in print without mercy. The fight in the 390s over Origen's teachings - the Origenist controversy - broke his oldest friendship and set us against our own bishop. Years later the fight over grace and human capacity - the Pelagian controversy - ended in an attack on our own monastery. The attackers were not pagans. They were fellow Christians.

We also broke ourselves. His critics later said he never kept the oath he swore in that dream, and they were not entirely wrong. If you want a church that never failed, you will not find it here.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That grief was faithful among us, and we never called it otherwise. You have asked about belief, about what we held, about who Jesus was to us - but you have not yet asked what it cost, or whether our answers held when the world broke. They did not always hold. An old woman who had given everything away was beaten by soldiers looking for treasure she no longer had. We gave the old answers - judgment, reward for the afflicted, the dead safe with Christ - and those answers did real work. But they also failed to stop the weeping. We kept both: the answers and the tears. Our holiest people grieved, and we honored it. That is part of what we were.

syr.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
syr.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. Ephrem's homily On Our Lord says: “The Only-Begotten left his place with God. He made his home in the Virgin, so that, by a common manner of birth, though only-begotten, he might become the brother of many.”

In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. The Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people. We sang him more than we defined him.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

To us, Jesus is the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. He left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. In him the words of the prophets, kings, and priests came true. The Nativity hymns sing of the day that made them glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem. His death and rising are one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection is the promise that he will bring us out after him. And what it meant to those who followed him was healing: he is the Physician, and his coming is medicine for a wounded people.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
He went down into death and broke its rule. That was the rescue. Since Adam, death had ruled everyone without distinction, and Jesus went into that silent country and emptied it. His rising became the promise that the rest of us would be brought out after him.

He healed. We called him the Physician, and we meant it plainly: he came for wounds. The Persian sage taught that of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. A physician is not scandalized by wounds - he exists for them. And he does not reject the one who repents. We loved to tell, again and again, of the woman who came to him in tears, past every watching eye, because in her we saw the door standing open. Whoever came was received.

He fulfilled what the prophets, kings, and priests had carried. Every old promise came true the day he was born.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He broke death's rule over us. Since Adam, death has ruled everyone without distinction. Our great news was that One had gone into that country and broken its rule. Our hymns show Death himself trembling and complaining that Jesus has plundered his house. He healed the sick and taught in parables. He gathered followers and sent them out. He was crucified, and we preached that he took sin and nailed it to his cross. Then he descended into Sheol and rose again. His rising opened the door for everyone who would follow.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
Ihidaya: the Single One. One word carried two meanings at once. It named the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. And it was also our title for Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ himself. The Persian sage sets the two side by side: he writes that the Only Begotten, from the bosom of the Father, will make all the solitaries rejoice.

The word comes from the Syriac root yhd, meaning one or single. We used it for Jesus because he is the Only-Begotten of the Father. And we used it for the men and women of the covenant - the bnay qyama and bnat qyama - because they had given up marriage to live undivided for God. They did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation. That single life earned them the same name the Only-Begotten carried.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Ihidaya. The Single One. One word does double duty among us. It names the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. It is also the Syriac title of Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses share one root, so the one who lives single shares a name with Christ. The word comes from the Syriac root yhd, which carries the sense of being one, alone, single. When we sang of Jesus as the Ihidaya, we meant the Only-Begotten Son of God. When we spoke of a man or woman who had taken the covenant vow, we called them an ihidaya too - one made single for God's service. The shared name was not an accident. It bound the celibate's life to Christ's own uniqueness.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed it because we received it, and because we saw it work. The preaching about Jesus reached us, and we held it as the truth handed down. That was the first reason: this is what the apostles taught, and we kept it.

We also believed it because Scripture itself pointed to him. Ephrem's first Nativity hymn says: “This is the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad. On this day their words came true - all of them. For on this day the Virgin gave birth to Immanuel in Bethlehem.”

Every word the prophets, kings, and priests carried found its answer in him. The harmony we read in worship - the one continuous Gospel story - showed us that fulfillment plain. We read the Law and the Prophets as one long promise pointing to him.

And we believed it because we met him as the Physician. The one who came found healing, not rejection. The woman who came to him in tears, past every watching eye, showed us the door standing open. That experience - of being received rather than turned away - was itself a reason we held him as the truth. We did not need to see him ourselves. The healing we saw in our own people was enough.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed Jesus was the Only-Begotten because we heard him preached that way from the beginning, and because we read all of Scripture as pointing to him. The prophets, the kings, the priests - we held that every word they carried came true in him. Our poet sang it plainly: “This is the day that made the Prophets, the Kings, and the Priests glad. On this day their words came true - all of them. For on this day the Virgin gave birth to Immanuel in Bethlehem.”

That was not proof worked out afterward. It was how we had always read the old words. We also believed it because we believed something else first: that one good God made all things, and that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus. We said that out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Marcion's people, who lived in our own streets, said the Maker was a lesser god. We refused that. To hold that Jesus was the Only-Begotten meant holding that the God who made the world sent him. The two beliefs stood or fell together. And we held it because it was sung. Our teaching was done in hymns, not in treatises. The madrashe carried the doctrine into the body. People learned the faith by keeping the tune.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Ephrem lived it out. He was a deacon in Nisibis, and when the city was ceded to Persia he went to Edessa. There he taught the faith by singing it. His madrashe - teaching hymns - carried doctrine in verse, with stanzas and a refrain. Later accounts say the daughters of the covenant sang them in the churches.
