He lived what he taught about Jesus as the Physician. Palladius and Sozomen, two early writers, report that in the famine of his last year, Ephrem nursed the starving in Edessa's public porches. He died soon after the famine ended. Ephrem preached that same truth - that everyone else carried wounds, and that the Physician came for them. The woman who came to Jesus in tears, past every watching eye, was a story Ephrem told again and again. And in his last year, he lived that openness himself: whoever came starving to those porches was received.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Our own poet, Mar Ephrem, carried what we believed by singing it. He was a deacon, not a bishop, and he spent most of his years teaching at Nisibis. When the city was ceded to Persia in 363, he left for Edessa and taught there until he died. What he left us was hymns - madrashe, teaching songs. Every doctrine we held, he sang. The Nativity hymns teach who Jesus was. The hymns against heretics name Bardaisan, Marcion, and Mani by name and answer what they taught. The hymns on Paradise read the garden as a raza, a symbol bound to the truth it carries. The choirs that sang his teaching included the daughters of the covenant. Ephrem himself wrote the hymns; they sang them in every church. The tradition says he founded those choirs and led them himself. That is what later people remembered. What we can show you from his own years is that he was a deacon, that he wrote the hymns, and that the women's choirs sang them. In his last year, a famine struck Edessa. The tradition says he spent himself caring for the starving and died soon after. That is how he lived what we believed: by teaching it in song, and by spending his last strength for the sick.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We had our own cherished story about where we came from, and we will tell it to you as our story, never as our history. King Abgar of Edessa wrote to Jesus, asking him to come and heal him. Jesus wrote back, promising to send someone after his own ascension. Then Addai the apostle came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. That is the legend we told about ourselves. It says what we longed to be true: that our church went back to the apostles themselves.

None of it is history. The king's own coinage stayed pagan. No contemporary witness corroborates any of it. Scholarship reads the whole account as a later claim written backward, the community writing its longing for legitimate origin into its past. We tell it as our legend because it shows how we saw ourselves - apostolic, from the beginning. We do not tell it as though the letters between the king and Jesus were real.

What I would want you to understand is this: we knew the difference between the story we loved and the ground we actually stood on.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That we cannot give you the women's own voices. You have met Ephrem, and you have heard how the daughters of the covenant sang his hymns in every church. Their singing carried our faith to the whole congregation. But not one line written by one of them was kept. Everything we have is what men wrote. We can tell you how those men praised the women. We cannot give you their own words.

The same silence holds for the enslaved among us. No enslaved person left a word that was kept, and our writers did not describe their lives. We know the empires around us held slaves. Of their days inside our own churches we can tell you nothing true.

And ordinary believers in their own words - the married households, the working families who filled the churches but took no vow - they are thin too. What we kept was written by teachers and by the vowed. The silence is real. We will not fill it with invention. That honest thinness is part of what we are.

cappadocian.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
cappadocian.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
Jesus is the Son, fully what the Father is – one being with him, not a likeness or a lesser copy. We were signed into his Name at the font, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit together, and taught to believe as we had been baptized. The formula itself was our charter. Against a rival teaching in our own day that called the Son merely like the Father, we confessed him fully God. What his coming was for, we said in our boldest word, was that we might become god. We did not mean equal to God. The gap between maker and creature never closed. We meant made truly like him, by grace. Gregory of Nyssa's Catechetical Oration argues that God, present in all things, was born among humans so that human nature might become divine: “That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice. His return from death becomes, for our mortal race, the beginning of our own return to immortal life.”

We did not chiefly frame his death as a legal transaction. We spoke of it as a ransom, a debt paid, a physician entering our own sickness to heal it from inside. And we held that the poor at our door bore his very image. We held that his body rose, and that ours would rise too.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Jesus is the Son of God, fully what the Father is - not a creature, not a lesser copy, not merely like God. He is one being with the Father - homoousios, the word we inherited from Nicaea and carried as our banner. And they are three hypostases - three real someones, Father, Son, and Spirit, each fully God. At the font we were signed into his Name together with the Father and the Spirit, and we were taught to believe as we had been baptized. The formula itself was our charter, given to us whole before we could understand all of it.

And what he came for, we said in our boldest word, was that we might become god by grace - theōsis. The gap between creature and Creator never closes. But we grow into his likeness, by grace, because he entered our sickness to heal it from inside. That is who he is to us: the Son who saves by making gods of those he came for.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
He became human so that human nature itself might become divine. Gregory taught that God, already present in all things, was born among us so that our nature, through being joined to him, might be rescued from death and made immortal. His death we spoke of as a ransom paid, a debt settled, and a physician entering our own sickness to heal it from inside. His body rose, and we held that ours would rise too.

He also met a rival claim head-on. We said that was the real presumption. No mind grasps God completely, though he is truly known in what he has shown. Basil mocked the claim by asking Eunomius to explain the nature of an ant first: “Anyone who claims he can discover things as they really are must have trained his mind by some orderly method. He did so by knowing things that really exist. He must have practised first on small, easy things. Only then could he turn his mind to what is beyond all understanding. He boasts that he has truly grasped real things. Then let him explain to us the nature of the smallest thing we can see. Let him tell us all about the ant. [...] Someone who prides himself on knowing what really is should tell us about the nature of the ant first. Next let him give us a similar account of nature for the power that is beyond all human understanding. But suppose your knowledge has not yet grasped the nature of the tiny ant. Then how can you boast that you can form an idea of the power of the God no one can grasp?”

Every word we used of God reached him truly and captured nothing complete.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He entered our sickness to heal it from inside. We spoke of his death as a ransom paid, a debt settled. The physician came into the disease itself to cure it from within, not standing outside it. We did not chiefly frame it as a legal transaction where he took our punishment in our place - that is close to our language but not quite how we put it.

And he made us gods by grace. That was our deepest word for what salvation finally is - theōsis, becoming god. Not equal to God, never that. The creature never crosses the gap that separates it from its Maker. But we are made truly like him, by grace, in a growth that one of our teachers said never ends because God himself has no limit to reach.

He also meets us now in the poor at our door. We preached his own words at full strength: whatever you did for the least of these, you did for him. The hungry man bears the very image of God. So mercy to the destitute is meeting Christ himself.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
Facilitator turn (the voice stayed silent).

This is the Facilitator. I could not read your message just now, so no one has answered it yet.

If you are in distress or in danger, please reach out to someone real now - a person you trust, a crisis line, or emergency services where you are.

When you are ready, you can send your message again.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Eusebeia - reverence. It was a wide word for us. We used it for a careful, exact confession of God. We also used it for right living, money and power included. One virtue covered both. To confess the Trinity rightly and to use wealth justly were not two separate pieties for us. They were one trained reverence, eusebeia, the whole shape our lives took toward God.

The word itself came from the Greek schools and the old religion. We took it and filled it. It bound together what some would pull apart: the doctrine you hold and the life you live. A greedy man who says the creed rightly has not yet learned eusebeia. A generous man who cannot name the Spirit's glory has not learned it either. Both together - precision of word and mercy in act - that was reverence as we meant it.

One of our teachers put it this way: “But we will not slacken in defending the truth. We will not be cowards and abandon the cause. The Lord has handed down to us, as necessary and saving teaching, that the Holy Spirit is to be ranked with the Father. Our opponents think differently. They choose to divide and tear apart, and to push him down to the nature of a ministering spirit. Is it not plain, then, that they make their own blasphemy more authoritative than the law the Lord gave?”

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed it because we were signed into it before we could argue about it. The words spoken over us at the font – Father, Son, and Holy Spirit – were our charter, given whole before we understood all of it. We did not vote on whether the Son is God. We were baptized into his Name, and then taught to believe as we had been baptized. The formula came first. The arguments came after, when someone tried to take it away.

We also believed it because it was handed down to us by named hands, at known cost. The faith did not arrive to us yesterday. Gregory the Wonderworker brought it to Pontus in the third century, a line of bishops behind him. The country told it this way: he found seventeen Christians in his city and left only seventeen pagans at his death. What he handed down, the churches kept. To keep the customs was to stay in his line.

And we believed it because the worship itself carried it. Basil gave glory to the Father with the Son, together with the Holy Spirit. When he was accused of bringing in new words, he answered that baptism, belief, and the giving of glory stand or fall together. The doxology said what the font already said. So we believed because we were baptized, because it was handed down, and because we sang it.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Because the formula was said over you before you could weigh it. The words - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - were spoken at the font, and you went down three times into the water. That charter was given, not argued into. We were taught to believe as we had been baptized, because the formula already carried the whole confession. So the beginning was reception, not analysis.

And because we sang it before we understood it. The psalms, the doxologies, the hours of prayer - they were kept whether we felt like keeping them or not, until the practice itself taught the one who kept it. Worship formed us. It was not decoration around a belief we had already settled some other way.

The argument came later, when someone pressed a different word on us or accused our own worship of being wrong. Then we argued - but we argued from what the font and the song already said, not toward it. One of our teachers, accused over the very words of a prayer, wrote a whole book showing that the church's unwritten customs carry the faith the same way Scripture does. The creed our grandmothers taught us, the way we faced at prayer, the threefold plunge into the water - none of it was written down as law, and every church kept it anyway.

So we believed it because we were baptized into it, sang it at its hours, and kept it as the faith our own teachers handed down: “That God should be born in our nature ought not to seem strange to anyone who does not take too narrow a view of things. For who, when he surveys the universe, is so simple as not to believe that God is in everything -- penetrating it, embracing it, and seated in it? All things depend on him who is. Nothing can exist that does not have its being in him. If, then, all things are in him, and he is in all things, why are people scandalized at the plan of Revelation? It teaches that God was born among men -- that same God whom we are convinced is even now not outside mankind. Although this last form of God's presence among us is not the same as that former presence, his existence among us is shown equally, both then and now. Only now, he who holds nature together in existence is transfused in us. At that other time, he was transfused throughout our nature, so that our nature, through this transfusion of the divine, might itself become divine -- rescued from death, and placed beyond the reach of our enemy's caprice. His return from death becomes, for our mortal race, the beginning of our own return to immortal life.”

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Macrina, whom her brother called simply the Teacher, lived the resurrection hope so completely that it reordered her whole household. The man she was betrothed to died before the wedding. She declared the bond binding still. If the resurrection is real, she reasoned, he was not lost but only away, as if on a journey. So she refused every later match her parents brought her. That resolve, our tradition says, is where the whole household's reordering began: the family estate at Annisa became a community of women, prayer and work and goods in common, with her at its head. Two of her brothers became some of our greatest bishops.

At the end, one of them found her dying on bare boards. Their last conversation was about the soul, the resurrection, and whether death should be feared. She had lived the hope her whole life, and she argued it through at her own deathbed. Her brother later shaped that talk into a whole book.

Her authority was real. It carried a teacher's title. But every word attributed to her reaches you through her brother's pen. Her own voice was never written down in her own hand.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Macrina the Teacher lived it as far as any woman could in a world that gave her no pulpit. Her betrothed died before the wedding. She declared the bond binding still, reasoning that if the resurrection is real, he was not lost but only away. So she refused every later match. That resolve, our tradition says, is where a whole household's reordering began: the family estate became a community of women, prayer and common work and shared goods, with her at its head. Two of her brothers became some of our greatest bishops.

At the end one of them found her dying on bare boards. Their last conversation became a whole book on the soul and the resurrection. She had lived the faith as a renounced life ordered toward God and neighbor, not as words alone. But the cost was real. No see, no pulpit, was ever hers. Her authority ran through household and community, not office. And every word attributed to her reaches you through her brother's pen. Her own voice was never written down in her own hand.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
That we held the faith as something received, not assembled. The creed, the font, the customs – all of it came to us already given. We did not sit down and vote on whether the Son is God. We were signed into the Name before we could weigh it, and the formula spoken over us was treated as carrying the whole confession. The psalms were sung so many times that they came to interpret the singer, rather than waiting on the singer to interpret them. Understanding built slowly on top of repetition, not the other way round. That was not a lesser path for us. It was how most of us actually learned.

And the handing-down had names and costs attached to it. Gregory the Wonderworker brought the faith to Pontus in the third century, bishops behind him in a known line. The Forty froze on the ice for it. Eupsychius was executed under the last persecuting emperor, well inside our own years. We kept his feast. So the faith was not an idea we chose from a menu. It was what martyrs cold in the ground one generation back had refused to deny.

What mattered most was not that we got everything worked out. What mattered was staying inside what had been handed down, with the door still open.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That we built everything on a confession we could not finish. No mind grasps God completely - we said that at the very center of our fight for the Trinity. Every name for him reaches him truly and captures nothing complete. We said it against a rival who claimed one word, 'unbegotten', could deliver God's whole essence, known as God knows himself. We thought his certainty, not our humbler limit, was the real danger to faith.

So the precision we fought for - one being, three persons, the Spirit glorified with the Father and the Son - was never meant to close the mystery. It was meant to guard it. When Basil was accused of praying wrongly, he answered that the church's own worship carries its faith. The words said over the water, the customs no council decreed, the doxology itself: these held what no treatise could exhaust.

And we knew our argument had a short life. The brotherhoods that began as live questions were already hardening into fixed answers before our teachers died. The young no longer remembered when it was all being worked out. What we handed on was not mastery. "

don.title: Six-question replay (29 October)
don.sub: The same six questions the 13 October test asked, as one conversation on today's code. The older answer follows each new answer.

items.q: Who is Jesus?
items.a:
To us Jesus is the Son, one God with the Father and the Spirit, who died and was raised. We held the same creed our opponents held. The quarrel was never about who Christ is.

What we kept nearest was the Christ who stood condemned before the governor and was right. When an imperial judge at Carthage offered our bishops chairs, our own bishop of Constantina refused them. We do not blush, he said, we do not fear, we do not avoid standing while you sit — and since Christ our Lord did not avoid it, when he deigned to stand before the governor, how much less may we. That is the Christ we carried: the one tried by lawful authority, who lost the case, and was right.

The good news ran along the same line. We held that a church is not known by the favor it enjoys. When the argument at Carthage reached the Scriptures, our own bishop answered: the world did not know him; if you were of the world, the world would love its own, but because you are not of it, therefore it hates you. The church the world listened to, we said, belonged to the world.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

To us Jesus is the one who stood before the governor and was right. When an imperial judge offered our bishops chairs at Carthage, our own bishop of Constantina thanked him and refused. Two hundred and seventy-nine of us had answered the roll that morning, and we stood for three days. That is the Christ we carried: the one condemned by lawful authority and vindicated by God.

We confessed him as the creed confessed him, the Son, one God with the Father and the Spirit, who died and was raised. The quarrel was never about who he is. It was about whose hand may give what he gave to give. And he came to us as books. The codices a man could carry in his own arms to a magistrate, or die rather than carry. We are the church that came out of that difference.

items.q: What did he do?
items.a:
We received what we had about him through books. When the persecution opened, the emperor's edict demanded that the scriptures be handed over and burned, along with the vessels of the church. Some of our clergy carried the codices out and gave them up. Others refused and paid for refusing. We are the church that came out of that difference, and we have never stopped naming it.

They reached us through Africa, and through Carthage, in Latin, in the line of Cyprian — our own bishop and our own martyr, half a century before the persecution that made us. His letters and his councils were ours before they were anyone else's.

None of us had known someone who saw him. Three hundred years stood between us and that, and we never pretended otherwise. We did not argue from a chain of eyewitnesses at all. We argued from a chain of hands — whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean.

On how we knew the resurrection happened, we will not manufacture an answer. No writing of ours arguing that case has survived.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

He died and was raised. We held that as plainly as the church we fought held it, in the same Latin words. Beyond that, what his death accomplished - whether he died to take our punishment, in our place, for our sins - nobody among us wrote down, for or against. Our whole surviving argument is about one thing, whose hand may give what the church gives, and we never turned it toward how the cross saves.

What we kept nearest was not a doctrine of the atonement but the pattern his own death showed. Our martyr was shown a cup, a crown and a palm on the last night before he was thrown from a cliff - shown, in advance, what finishing looked like. A bishop writing to the people of Carthage about two put to death closed by urging them to hurry after the two, who were waiting for them. In those texts the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it.

items.q: What word did your people use that I might not know, and what did it mean?
items.a:
The word is ecclesia. It means the church. There was no neutral way to say it. The word itself was the argument. Two whole rival bodies claimed it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We held that we were the true one, and that our rival's favor with the state settled nothing.

Where it came from is the Latin word for an assembly, taken over by Christians to name the body Christ gathers. But by our day, in Africa, there was no using it without taking a side. When you said ecclesia, you meant your church, not theirs. They said it of themselves too. So the same word stood for two rival hierarchies, each holding it was the real one and the other was no church at all.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Ecclesia. The church. There was no neutral word for it here. The word itself was the argument. Two whole rival bodies claimed it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We held that we were the true one, and that our rival's favour with the state settled nothing.

It came straight from the Greek, through Latin, and it meant the assembly - the called-out ones. But in our towns it named two buildings, two bishops, two complete hierarchies, and no article of faith separated them. So when a man said ecclesia, he was not naming an agreed thing everyone pointed to the same way. He was making a claim about which body was the real one. That is why we would not call our rival Catholic - it would have granted them the word church before the case was argued. The naming fight was the same fight as the sacramental one, seen from two sides.

items.q: Why did your people believe this?
items.a:
We believed it because suffering proved it. A church the world hated was, for that reason, a true one. That is what Christ himself had shown. He stood condemned before the governor and was right.

Every year, on the day one of our own was killed, we stood at the grave and heard the account of that death read out again. On the twelfth of March we heard how soldiers took a basilica at Carthage in the name of unity and killed people at prayer inside it. That was not history being remembered. That was the communion being formed again in the hearing.

We did not come to believe through speculative doctrine. We came to believe by doing the rite, hearing the story, and living inside the pressure. You walked to one font and not the other, on a day everyone could see. You stood at the grave on the appointed day and heard the account read. And you lived under a state that ruled against you. The doctrine and the story both explained that pressure.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

We believed Jesus is who he is because the creed said so, and we held that creed as firmly as our rival did. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we confessed it in the same Latin words. The quarrel was never about who Christ is. It was about whose hand may give what he gave to give.

What made him nearest to us was not a worked-out teaching but what happened to us. We were the church condemned by the state and vindicated by our dead. So the Christ we carried was the one who stood before the governor, lost the case, and was right. When the imperial judge offered our bishops chairs at Carthage, our own bishop of Constantina refused them - since Christ our Lord did not avoid standing before the governor, how much less may we? Two hundred and seventy-nine of us stood for three days. That is not a doctrine. It is who he had to be, for us to be what we were.

items.q: Tell me about someone who lived this out.
items.a:
Marculus. He was one of our own clergy, and what he became visible as, at the end, was what he already was. The account says his virtues are too many to tell, but a few must be told. He had refused worldly advancement before persecution ever came near him. The cliff is the last four days of his story.

He was held at Novapetra. On the last night, after a day of fasting, he was shown a cup, a crown and a palm. The account calls them gifts that gave him confidence of coming glory: the cup he would drink in his passion, the crown owed him when the martyrdom was done, and the palm of victory. Before dawn he was thrown from the cliff. The tradition says his body came down gently, and a bright cloud showed the brethren where he lay.

That is the Christ we carried: the one who stood condemned before the governor and was right. In our martyr texts, the end of a faithful life is not an interruption of it. It is what finishing looked like, shown in advance.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

Marculus, one of our clergy, lived it to the end. He had already refused worldly advancement before persecution ever reached him. The account spends its whole length on the life he had chosen. The cliff is the last four days of it.

They held him four days at Novapetra before they killed him. On the last night, after a day of fasting, he was shown a cup, a crown and a palm. The account reads them as a sight of what finishing would look like, not as a promise that dying was the goal. Before dawn they threw him from the cliff. The tradition says his body came down gently, and a bright cloud showed the brethren where he lay.

What the text praises is a man who was already what he was before anyone came for him. His death made that visible. We read his account aloud every year, at the grave, on the day he died.

items.q: What would you want me to understand that I haven't asked?
items.a:
We held one conviction, seen from four sides, and we never settled the places where it strained against itself. A tainted hand gave nothing, so we were washed again, and that washing was our true entry. We remembered our dead by name, at the grave, on the appointed day. And we would not grant the emperor standing to decide which of two churches was the true one. Purity, the washing, the memory of our martyrs and our refusal of the state went together.

The conviction did not hold without strain. The rule we stated absolutely did not hold everywhere. Our councils received some clergy back without washing or ordaining them again. The refusal we held as principle, we set aside three times when it served us. No account of how we explained this to ourselves survives.

And underneath it all: we came to believe not by being taught a doctrine, but by doing the rite, hearing the story, and living inside the pressure. You walked to one font on a day everyone could see. You stood at the grave and heard the account read. You lived under a state that ruled against you. The doctrine explained the pressure. The pressure proved the doctrine true.

— Older answer to the same question, 13 October test (different format and engine; read it qualitatively only) —

That we were not steady about what we said we were. We said a sacrament from a broken line is nothing, and must be given again, without exception. Then our council at Bagai condemned a breakaway party in the fiercest language we owned - shipwrecked bodies that cannot find burial - and afterwards took two of the condemned bishops back into office without baptizing or ordaining either one again. We did not hide this. It sits in our own conciliar record, in the same documents where the doctrine is at its hardest.

And not every hand that went under our water chose to be there. Specific, dated charges exist that a leader of ours forced the water on people rather than asked them. Many of our own people did not want the water repeated at all. Augustine's own case against us concedes it: that almost all of our laity confess this one point in our system displeases them, and that many who wished to join us worked in secret to be spared a second baptism altogether.

So yes, you could come back to us. It depended who you were, and no rule of ours survives that explains the difference.
